question: Can a single distance-only procedure infer locally adaptive unweighted neighborhoods, pointwise Gaussian bandwidths, manifold embeddings, graph geodesics, and varying local intrinsic dimension without being given a global neighbor count, sampling density, dimension, reach, or boundary?

key_findings.claim: IAN alternates a conservative discrete graph with a globally coupled continuous cover, then removes edges whose required scales are anomalous relative to the rest of the sample.
key_findings.evidence: Algorithm 1 starts from the exact Gabriel graph, assigns one scale per point by minimizing their sum subject to edge-covering constraints, forms the symmetric kernel K_ij=exp(-||x_i-x_j||^2/(sigma_i sigma_j)), computes a normalized continuous-to-discrete volume ratio, and deletes an outlying node's farthest edge. The procedure needs only a complete pairwise distance matrix in its exact route. The paper also gives a greedy scale-splitting alternative when the linear program is expensive.

key_findings.claim: The scale optimization preserves edge covering, but the paper mislabels its convexification and provides no approximation guarantee for the resulting minimum.
key_findings.evidence: The original feasible set sigma_i sigma_j >= (C r_ij)^2 inside pointwise upper bounds is nonconvex. Secant or tangent half-spaces retain only scale pairs on the covering side of each hyperbola, so the construction is an inner approximation of the feasible set with the same L1 objective. Calling this a relaxation in which 'only the objective is relaxed' is backwards: the objective is unchanged and the constraints are strengthened. Covering is consequently preserved, but no factor or additive bound relates the LP optimum to the original nonconvex optimum; the appendix's greedy solver is likewise explicitly suboptimal.

key_findings.claim: The normalized volume ratio is an interpretable heuristic, not a validated estimator or a consequence of manifold consistency theory.
key_findings.evidence: The derivation approximates a local Gaussian integral by (sqrt(pi) sigma_i)^d, treats the discrete degree as a unit-height hypercube volume, substitutes the empirical relation deg(i) approximately 2^d, estimates dimension by log2 deg(i), and expects sigma_i to match a local-volume radius. Each step assumes local uniformity, low curvature, small bandwidth, adequate sampling, and approximately correct current edges. The 2^d law is supported only by simulated regular, jittered, uniform, and normal point clouds in Figures 9 and 12. The authors explicitly say several implied bounds and Laplacian convergence of their kernel remain to be proved.

key_findings.claim: Finite edge deletion guarantees termination, not recovery of the true topology, connectivity, or a statistically calibrated stopping point.
key_findings.evidence: Every nonterminal iteration deletes at least one edge, so a finite graph must stop. That proof does not show that deleted edges are false or retained edges are true. The paper acknowledges that sparse Swiss-cheese samples retain edges across real holes and says connectivity, when required, must be enforced by stopping pruning before disconnection. The weighted graph is called connected only up to a numerical tolerance because its complete Gaussian weights can underflow. The 4.5-standard-deviation C3 rule is selected empirically and may be judged interactively by the user.

key_findings.claim: The paper's claim of having no free parameter beyond an outlier requirement understates several consequential thresholds and choices.
key_findings.evidence: The experiments fix the C3 threshold at 4.5 estimated standard deviations, choose how many outlying edges to prune per iteration, retune C when the median departs sufficiently from one, optionally stop on multiscale ratios, choose an extended-neighborhood hop count for NCD, and optimize a heat-diffusion time separately for each geodesic dataset. The artifact adds defaults max_prune=0.1, a hard minimum threshold 2.75, a moving maximum threshold near 5, median tolerance 0.1, initial C clipped to [0.55,0.95], and optional approximate-kNN size and connectivity policy. These may be robust defaults, but they are parameters or discrete design choices whose sensitivity is not systematically reported.

key_findings.claim: The empirical evidence shows useful adaptive behavior on purpose-built synthetic manifolds, but does not support the universal statement that IAN dominates in all cases.
key_findings.evidence: Figures 24-28 compare graph appearance and embeddings across selected k values on stingray, spiral, and bent-plane examples, chiefly by visual judgment. The stochastic t-SNE and UMAP experiments are each run once with one shared seed, so there are no uncertainty estimates. The five-dimensional cylinder is the only embedding experiment with a numeric score: Kendall tau is 0.97 for IAN plus diffusion maps, 0.83 versus 0.86 for UMAP versus IAN+UMAP, and 0.82 versus 0.83 for t-SNE versus IAN+t-SNE; the text separately reports Isomap tau=0.98. Geodesics are qualitative color plots without distance error, and NCD is compared mainly against one MLE family. These are informative demonstrations, not a broad benchmark over real data or current methods.

key_findings.claim: NCD adapts a correlation-dimension curve to graph-defined local neighborhoods and corrects boundary bias by recentering, but its best reported high-dimensional result still underestimates dimension.
key_findings.evidence: For each point, NCD evaluates the slope of log Z_i against log sigma over an extended graph neighborhood, takes the highest local maximum, recenters on a nearby node with minimum median squared distance, averages immediate-neighbor estimates, and finally takes the maximum with a smoothed floor(log2 degree) estimate. On the stingray and bent plane, the displayed local dimensions follow the constructed geometry. On the R x S^4 cylinder with N=8403, IAN+NCD reports mean 4.63 for true d=5 while MLE at k=32 reports 4.86. The paper attributes NCD's bias to sample size and points to an a-posteriori correction that it does not apply.

key_findings.claim: Three rendered equations contain material printed defects, and the reach statement omits the bottleneck term that can reverse its claimed bound.
key_findings.evidence: Equation (41) prints the Levina-Bickel MLE average of log distance ratios without the required outer reciprocal, so as written it estimates inverse dimension. In the NCD derivation, equation (43) prints Z approximately N^2(sqrt(2pi)sigma)^d/vol(M)^2, while the very next logarithmic equation (44) has only one power of vol(M); direct integration under a uniform distribution confirms the latter denominator. Earlier, the paper says the reach is lower-bounded by 1/kappa_max. A curvature cap alone lower-bounds the local radius of curvature, but reach is also limited by half a bottleneck distance and can therefore be smaller. All three issues are present in the exact rendered PDF and native v3 TeX, not extraction artifacts.

key_findings.claim: The official artifact is a useful implementation and demo collection, but the paper-era tag is not a portable frozen reproduction of the paper.
key_findings.evidence: The official repository's v1.0.0 tag is dated 2023-01-09, two days after arXiv v3, and builds a wheel. In a clean temporary Python 3.10 environment with current dependencies, exact five-point greedy and L1 smoke tests pass. However, v1.0.0's stingray generator fails under NumPy 2 because it calls removed ndarray.ptp, and its approximate route fails with NameError because knndists was not imported; both were fixed only later. Post-release commits also fix sparse diffusion-map thresholding and insert a missing factor 1/2 in graph divergence for heat geodesics. Thus the release contemporaneous with the paper does not preserve a fully working current environment and contains a numerical geodesic defect.

key_findings.claim: The artifact's greedy solver does not implement the appendix's defining longest-edge-first order, so its high-dimensional greedy results are not literal executions of the published algorithm.
key_findings.evidence: The appendix specifies processing candidate edges in decreasing Euclidean length because scale assignments are updated sequentially. In both v1.0.0 and current main, however, the Cython greedySplitting routine iterates weighted_edges.items() without sorting, while its caller constructs that dictionary directly from scipy.sparse.find on the upper-triangular adjacency, which yields coordinate rather than distance order. The cylinder notebook explicitly selects obj='greedy' for its 8,403-point run. Because later edges can rescale already assigned endpoints or transfer excess scale between them, this undocumented order is algorithmically consequential; no evidence establishes that the stored figure used the appendix's stated ordering.

key_findings.claim: Current main executes the core pipeline but still contains untested broken helper routes and cannot regenerate the complete paper from a clean scripted workflow.
key_findings.evidence: Audited main commit 06606ab27b52a1ea60daebae082a0e6752625521 builds as version 1.1.2; py_compile passes, exact five-point greedy/L1 tests pass, and an exact 200-point spiral run completes IAN, NCD, and heat geodesics with finite outputs. Yet computeTSNEkernel with its default normalize=True raises NameError because it asserts on undefined P, computeTSNEsigmas on a sparse matrix raises NameError because it refers to undefined D2, and plotScales refers to undefined edge_list when its midpoint-scale branch is requested. The repository has four executed synthetic notebooks with no stored error outputs, but no tests, CI, environment lock, exact dependency versions, raw tables, figure-generation script, or notebooks for every figure/data family. The notebooks rely on private UMAP internals, the embedding helpers also call private scikit-learn APIs, and the examples manually compose max(NCD,degree) while the public NCD function returns the components separately.

method.core_idea: Infer a graph from distance geometry without fixing one global neighborhood size: begin with every Gabriel edge that has no closer witness in its diametral ball, globally choose the smallest pointwise Gaussian scales that cover those edges, and iteratively prune relatively distant edges revealed by anomalously large local kernel volume.
method.mechanism: Gabriel geometry supplies a scale-free candidate graph. Hyperbolic pairwise covering requirements are conservatively linearized and solved by an L1 linear program, or approximated greedily. A point's single-scale Gaussian weighted degree is normalized by its unweighted degree and the empirical Gabriel relation degree approximately 2^d; robust distributional outliers lose their farthest edge. The converged unweighted and weighted graphs are then substituted into existing embedding, heat-geodesic, and local-dimension procedures.
assumptions: Input distances are meaningful Euclidean or metric-space proxies for local manifold geometry; the exact algorithm has access to the complete pairwise matrix.
The sample is locally uniform enough that neighbor-distance variability is a dataset-wide bias removable by one global C, even if density changes over the manifold.
At the kernel scale, curvature is low, the manifold resembles a tangent Euclidean space, dimension is locally stable, and enough points populate each local volume element.

Gabriel degree is approximately centered at 2^d for generic interior sampling, including after iterative pruning; boundary, lattice, wheel, sparse, noisy, and intersecting configurations can violate this relation.
A false long edge inflates one endpoint's optimized scale and normalized volume ratio enough to become a robust upper-tail outlier before true edges are removed.
The C3 quartile model and fixed 4.5-standard-deviation cutoff are appropriate despite dependence between node statistics and potentially multimodal or heavy-tailed distributions.

For NCD, an extended graph neighborhood stays on one manifold sheet, contains enough nearly uniform points, and does not cross an abrupt dimension transition; recentering does not change the target dimension.
The selected synthetic manifolds and manually chosen embedding/kernel integrations are representative of wider real-data behavior.
A finite deletion sequence is treated as an adequate optimization path even though deletions are irreversible and the result can depend on threshold and pruning batch size.

techniques.role: Builds a scale-invariant superset of plausible local edges from pairwise squared-distance tests.
Couples pointwise Gaussian bandwidths through product constraints on every current edge.
Replaces hyperbolic feasible regions by conservative secant/tangent half-spaces and minimizes the L1 sum of scales.
Provides a cheaper largest-edge-first scale assignment with rebalancing against farthest-neighbor upper bounds.
Compares a node's single-scale Gaussian mass with its discrete degree after a degree-based dimension normalization.
Uses a quartile-derived location and dispersion estimate to identify outliers and delete their farthest incident edges.
Substitutes the learned graph or bandwidths into diffusion maps, Isomap, t-SNE, and UMAP.
Estimates pointwise dimension from maxima of local correlation-slope curves over recentered multi-hop graph neighborhoods.
Applies a discrete heat method to the learned weighted graph for geodesic estimates.

evaluations.setting: Regular, jittered, uniform-random, and normal-random point clouds through intrinsic dimension 8
evaluations.result: Figures 9 and 12 visually support mean degree approximately 2^d for generic samples; exact lattices and boundaries are explicit exceptions
evaluations.baseline: The empirical 2^d curve used later as a normalization and local-dimension proxy

evaluations.setting: Horseshoe, limb, three-cluster, and bent-plane synthetic datasets
evaluations.metric: Iteration histories of normalized volume ratios, scales, and deleted edges
evaluations.result: Figures 19-22 show high-ratio nodes tracking designed cross-gap edges and convergence after those edges are removed

evaluations.metric: Visual preservation of five true holes
evaluations.result: Dense samples recover holes, whereas the sparse sample retains edges through some holes, directly displaying an information-limit failure
evaluations.baseline: Initial Gabriel graph and known hole outlines

evaluations.setting: Stingray with dimension changing from a two-dimensional body to a one-dimensional tail
evaluations.result: IAN covers most of the body while keeping the tail nearly minimal; kNN, t-SNE, UMAP, self-tuning, and variable-bandwidth kernels trade body holes against tail short circuits across k=2,4,8,16,32
evaluations.baseline: Five global neighborhood sizes for each compared kernel

evaluations.setting: Stingray, spiral, and bent-plane embedding demonstrations
evaluations.result: Using the IAN graph or scales generally yields visually reasonable outputs across diffusion maps, variable-bandwidth diffusion, Isomap, t-SNE, and UMAP, but no embedding-quality statistic or repeated-run uncertainty is supplied
evaluations.baseline: Each embedding method over five selected k values

evaluations.setting: Uniform random five-dimensional cylinder R x S^4 with N=8403 in R^6
evaluations.metric: Kendall tau of order along the cylinder axis
evaluations.result: Figure 29 reports tau=0.97 for IAN+diffusion maps, 0.83 versus 0.86 for UMAP versus IAN+UMAP, and 0.82 versus 0.83 for t-SNE versus IAN+t-SNE; the text reports Isomap tau=0.98
evaluations.baseline: UMAP and t-SNE with k=27 chosen from IAN's mean degree, plus qualitative self-tuning and variable-bandwidth comparisons

evaluations.metric: Visual agreement of heat or graph geodesic color fields with ground truth
evaluations.result: IAN heat and unweighted graph geodesics look close to the ground truth, while several k/kernel choices short-circuit; no numerical distance error is reported and heat time is optimized per dataset
evaluations.baseline: kNN graph geodesics and weighted graphs from t-SNE, UMAP, self-tuning, and variable-bandwidth kernels

evaluations.setting: Stingray, bent plane, five-dimensional cylinder, tiara, and spinning-top local-dimension examples
evaluations.metric: Pointwise dimension plots and mean estimates
evaluations.result: IAN+NCD tracks designed varying dimension visually; on the cylinder it averages 4.63 for true d=5, below MLE's 4.86 at k=32
evaluations.baseline: NCD and Levina-Bickel MLE over selected global k values

evaluations.setting: Official repository v1.0.0 and main commit 06606ab27b52a1ea60daebae082a0e6752625521
evaluations.metric: Build, import, smoke, example, and source-consistency audit
evaluations.result: Both tags build wheels and exact five-point IAN runs; current main also completes a finite exact 200-point spiral IAN/NCD/heat run, while v1.0.0 fails current stingray and approximate routes and current main has two reproducible t-SNE helper NameErrors

limitations: Author-stated: several geometric bounds and convergence of the learned multiscale kernel to an appropriate Laplacian operator remain conjectural and need proof.
Author-stated: sparse samples cannot reveal all holes, and pruning may need to stop early when connected output is required.
Reviewer-identified: the volume-ratio derivation combines several asymptotic approximations with an empirical degree law, but the outlier threshold is treated as if quantitatively calibrated.
Reviewer-identified: edge deletion is irreversible, and termination proves neither topological correctness nor optimality of the final graph.

Reviewer-identified: exact Gabriel construction and full distance/kernel matrices are quadratic in storage and at least quadratic in work; the approximate route reintroduces a neighborhood-size parameter and has weaker Gabriel guarantees.

Reviewer-identified: the paper tests synthetic datasets almost exclusively, reports qualitative plots for most tasks, and gives no repeated-seed uncertainty, statistical tests, real-data benchmarks, or runtime/memory scaling table.
Reviewer-identified: comparison baselines are largely methods already cited before 2022; CkNN, ABID, Gride, later learned adaptive graphs, LocalMAP, and current LID benchmarks are absent.
Reviewer-identified: the heat method uses uniform node areas and a tuned diffusion time, even though local dimension and sampling density are precisely the quantities the paper argues are variable.
Reviewer-identified: NCD requires a hop count and can blur true dimension transitions through recentering and neighbor averaging; its cylinder result retains finite-sample downward bias.

Reviewer-identified: the official artifact is a small research codebase with no tests, CI, lockfile, raw result archive, or complete paper-figure pipeline, and both historical and current defects affect advertised routes.

Reviewer-identified: the implementation never sorts edges by decreasing length before greedy splitting, contrary to the appendix; order-sensitive greedy results, including the cylinder example, therefore lack source-level fidelity to the stated algorithm.
failure_modes: Uniformly sparse sampling makes real holes indistinguishable from ordinary gaps, so IAN can retain topologically false edges.
A heavy-tailed or multimodal but legitimate distribution of local spacings can make the global C correction and C3 cutoff prune true low-density connections.
Wheel-like or highly symmetric configurations can give arbitrarily many Gabriel neighbors, breaking the degree approximately 2^d proxy and volume normalization.
Boundaries reduce degree and asymmetric neighborhoods; replacing degree one by two and smoothing nearby estimates does not remove all boundary bias.
Close manifold sheets, bottlenecks, intersections, high curvature, or abrupt dimension changes can create Gabriel edges that are not globally anomalous enough to prune.
Large pruning batches can delete multiple mutually dependent edges before statistics are recomputed, changing the result or disconnecting nodes.
Approximate kNN distance input can omit witnesses needed by the Gabriel test or true candidate edges; MST repair changes the graph construction and depends on a user-selected maximum neighborhood.
The NCD slope curve can have multiple or numerically unstable maxima when an extended neighborhood is nonuniform, too small, noisy, mixed-dimensional, or truncated by a boundary.

The paper-era artifact fails its approximate route and one showcased dataset under current NumPy, while current t-SNE helper defaults, sparse scale estimation, and one plotting branch raise NameError.

Greedy scale splitting is order-dependent, but both the publication-era and current implementations traverse coordinate-ordered sparse edges rather than the appendix's required decreasing-length order.
reusable_insights: Separate a discrete neighborhood hypothesis from a continuous kernel cover and use disagreement between them as a diagnostic signal.
A product-bandwidth kernel makes pairwise covering constraints globally coupled while retaining one interpretable scale per node.
When a nonconvex constraint must never be violated, an inner polyhedral approximation can preserve safety even though it is not an optimization relaxation in the usual sense.
Graph-defined multi-hop neighborhoods can expand sample size for local estimators without naïvely taking a larger ambient-space ball that crosses folds.
Visualizing the complete distribution and iteration history of a pruning statistic is more informative than reporting only a final graph.
A useful artifact audit should test both the publication-era release and current main: later fixes can improve portability while changing the numerical method used for a published result.
For sequential greedy algorithms, edge or sample ordering is part of the method and must be stated, implemented explicitly, and covered by a source-consistency test.

Adaptive neighborhood methods need evaluation that independently stresses density, curvature, boundary, bottlenecks, noise, dimension changes, and finite sample size rather than combining them only in attractive toy plots.
open_questions: Under what sampling, reach, density, and boundary conditions does IAN recover the correct neighborhood graph or homology with high probability?
Does the learned multiscale kernel converge to a specified Laplace-Beltrami or density-corrected operator, and at what finite-sample rate?
Can the empirical Gabriel degree law around 2^d be proved or replaced by a calibrated local estimator that handles boundaries and non-Poisson samples?
What false-deletion and false-retention rates does the C3 volume-ratio rule achieve under dependence between nodes, and can its threshold be selected with error control?
How sensitive are final graphs to the inner LP approximation, C search interval, median tolerance, pruning batch size, solver tolerance, and edge-deletion order?
Can a connectivity or topology constraint be built into optimization instead of relying on interactive early stopping?
How does IAN compare quantitatively with CkNN, modern adaptive density graphs, LocalMAP, ABID/Gride, and learned graph generators on current real and synthetic benchmarks?
Can NCD be reformulated with uncertainty intervals and adaptive hop selection while preserving abrupt local dimension transitions?
Do area- and dimension-aware discrete differential operators improve the graph heat geodesics, and can diffusion time be selected without ground truth?
Which exact code revision produced each published figure, especially the heat-geodesic panels predating the divergence correction?

competitive_landscape.title: Variable Bandwidth Diffusion Kernels
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest prior theory for density-adaptive symmetric Gaussian kernels and graph-Laplacian convergence.
competitive_landscape.difference: Berry and Harlim choose bandwidths from estimated sampling density and derive asymptotic expansions and pointwise errors, including noncompact settings. IAN instead infers scales jointly from a pruned Gabriel cover and handles varying apparent dimension empirically, but does not prove an operator limit.

competitive_landscape.title: Consistent Manifold Representation for Topological Data Analysis
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct prior adaptive unweighted graph construction for nonuniform manifold samples.
competitive_landscape.difference: CkNN connects i and j when distance is below a global delta times the geometric mean of their kth-neighbor radii and proves geometric consistency under conditions. It retains global k and delta, whereas IAN seeks data-driven pointwise neighborhoods without known dimension; conversely IAN lacks CkNN's consistency theory.

competitive_landscape.title: UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction
competitive_landscape.relationship: Primary scalable manifold-embedding baseline whose local fuzzy graph IAN can replace.
competitive_landscape.difference: UMAP uses a user-selected n_neighbors and optimizes a low-dimensional fuzzy-set cross entropy with a mature scalable implementation. IAN concentrates on estimating the input graph and scales, then injects them into UMAP; its evidence is small synthetic geometry rather than UMAP's breadth and scalability.

competitive_landscape.title: ABID: Angle Based Intrinsic Dimensionality
competitive_landscape.relationship: Contemporaneous local intrinsic-dimension competitor based on neighborhood geometry rather than distance growth.
competitive_landscape.difference: ABID derives estimators from pairwise angle distributions and reports robustness on noise and intersecting subspaces, but still requires a neighborhood. NCD uses distance-only graph neighborhoods and correlation slopes, making it applicable without coordinates while inheriting IAN's graph and degree assumptions.

competitive_landscape.title: Distributional Results for Model-Based Intrinsic Dimension Estimators
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest contemporaneous statistically derived multiscale intrinsic-dimension estimator.
competitive_landscape.difference: Cride/Gride generalize TwoNN through exact distributions of neighbor-distance ratios, expose scale dependence, and improve noise robustness. IAN+NCD focuses on varying pointwise dimension and graph-defined tubular neighborhoods, but supplies neither likelihood uncertainty nor a head-to-head comparison with Gride.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Adaptive Neighborhoods for Graph Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Post-publication adaptive-neighborhood graph learner with pointwise neighborhood sizes.
competitive_landscape.difference: Saha et al.'s differentiable graph generator learns topology jointly with a supervised downstream GNN and scales to trajectory, point-cloud, and node-classification tasks. IAN is unsupervised, distance-only, and geometrically interpretable, but is not end-to-end task-adaptive and has weaker scaling evidence.

competitive_landscape.title: Dimension Reduction with Locally Adjusted Graphs
competitive_landscape.relationship: Post-publication direct competitor that dynamically modifies local graph structure during dimensionality reduction.
competitive_landscape.difference: LocalMAP updates graph forces on dynamically extracted subgraphs to improve cluster separation in large biological datasets. IAN estimates a reusable input graph before embedding and targets manifold geometry, geodesics, and dimension, whereas LocalMAP is embedding-objective-specific and validated on real clustering use cases.

competitive_landscape.title: Manifold Dimension Estimation Via Local Graph Structure
competitive_landscape.relationship: Current local graph-based manifold dimension estimator.
competitive_landscape.difference: The 2026 revision explicitly combines local graph structure with PCA and regression-based estimation. It targets dimension rather than graph recovery and arrives after IAN, but provides a current graph-local alternative to NCD's correlation-slope and degree-max construction.

competitive_landscape.title: A Connection Between Score Matching and Local Intrinsic Dimension
competitive_landscape.difference: Yeats et al. relate denoising and implicit score-matching losses to LID and benchmark diffusion-model estimators at large problem sizes. The method requires a trained generative model rather than only distances; IAN+NCD is lightweight and geometric but was not evaluated on modern high-dimensional image manifolds or memory scaling.

competitive_landscape.title: Why We Need New Benchmarks for Local Intrinsic Dimension Estimation
competitive_landscape.relationship: Current official benchmark framework that directly challenges conclusions drawn from simple synthetic LID tests.
competitive_landscape.difference: Tempczyk et al. preserve one manifold across multiple domain representations and apply controlled stressors, finding that success on simple manifolds does not transfer and state-of-the-art estimators fail targeted cases. IAN's NCD evidence uses hand-designed low-dimensional geometry and would need this kind of cross-domain stress test to establish current competitiveness.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim a data-driven, parameter-light neighborhood kernel that adapts jointly to sampling density, local geometry, and varying intrinsic dimension, improves several manifold-learning algorithms, and supplies a new local dimension estimator without a fixed k.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The distinctive construction is the iterative loop between a Gabriel graph, globally optimized pointwise Gaussian covering scales, and a normalized volume-ratio edge-pruning statistic. Figures 19-35 demonstrate this loop across graph recovery, embeddings, geodesics, and pointwise dimension, and the official code implements all four core components.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The durable novelty is the explicit discrete-continuous consistency loop and its reuse across several manifold tasks, not a theorem of parameter-free manifold recovery or universal empirical dominance. Prior variable-bandwidth and CkNN work offered stronger asymptotic guarantees with fixed neighborhood controls; contemporaneous ABID/Gride offered more statistically grounded dimension estimators; later learned adaptive graphs, LocalMAP, graph-PCA estimators, neural LID methods, and harder benchmarks broaden the competitive field. IAN remains an original geometric research prototype whose main statistic, threshold calibration, topology recovery, and operator limit are open.

reviewer_notes: Primary pass used the exact 68-page arXiv v3 PDF whose fresh SHA-256 matched the atlas pin, the pinned pypdf+tesseract extraction with usable text on 67 pages, and the exact v3 native source tarball (SHA-256 8a6fb03ca42a59ab582c94b0ac3aae1e086bc743400e2a6a5f8a30c69d3533be) containing all section TeX and 35 figure PDFs. Every PDF page was raster-inspected; OCR-missing page 15 was reopened at full-page resolution and confirmed as the first half of Figure 6, and key degree, tuning, graph, embedding, geodesic, and dimension figures were separately rendered at high resolution. Formula checks covered the Gabriel rule and curvature equations (14)-(17), covering and LP equations (18)-(27), volume equations (28)-(40), MLE equation (41), NCD equations (42)-(51), and the complete greedy appendix. The official GitHub repository was freshly cloned and inspected at paper-adjacent tag v1.0.0 (fc849930c2837d96831f022a41324de7bc533561) and current main commit 06606ab27b52a1ea60daebae082a0e6752625521, including all 3,966 Python/Cython source lines, four notebooks and stored outputs, README/setup/license, full commit history, tags, dependency metadata, and post-release fixes. Both revisions built wheels; exact greedy/L1 smoke tests passed, a current exact spiral IAN/NCD/heat run produced finite output, and targeted runtime tests reproduced the reported historical and current defects. Full notebook regeneration was not attempted because the repository does not pin an environment, the cylinder run materializes an approximately 8403-by-8403 distance matrix, and the notebooks depend on version-sensitive private UMAP APIs; their stored cells and outputs were inspected instead. Current competitors were checked against primary arXiv records or official proceedings through 2026-08-24. This is an honest primary full-text reading, not an independently verified second pass.
